representative_reviews.title: To the Moon
representative_reviews.text: To the Moon sits in a very distinct category as far as games go. It is focused on story and emotion. The game mechanics are not important; you are not being punished for doing anything wrong during a puzzle, so leave your competitive side at the door when you press play. The game takes some ideas from Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, but it still feels original. This comparison should give away the main concept of the game. If you loved the movie, I am sure you will also love this game. The music, composed by Kan Gao, also the creator of the game, is amazing. It fits the game perfectly; it never feels boring, even if you stay in the same scene for minutes. The songs have a calming, homey feel that never becomes annoying despite their repetition. The art matches the story; it always surprises me how pixel art can show a character's emotions so well. The colours remind me of autumn, and everything feels very atmospheric. It's a beautiful game to look at. I want to underline that, as with all different mediums of art, games can also have an emotional impact, and To the Moon will work your tear ducts to the maximum. Have some tissues ready, just in case.

representative_reviews.title: Finding Paradise
representative_reviews.text: [h2]A solid addition to the world of "To the moon"[/h2] I think if I had to pick, I'd probably say I preferred to the moon, but that could just as well be because I played it first, it's not uncommon to be biased towards your introductory game or episode of a series. I thought this was pretty sweet, it's still a narrative game with some puzzle elements, but the writing is great, if the writing wasn't as top tier as it is I definitely wouldn't have enjoyed this or to the moon one bit, and for a dyslexic person who struggles to maintain focus when reading, that says a lot to it's quality. The sprites are mostly just the same as to the moon, but still just as amazing, I did notice some weird mixels during Neil's transformation sequence, and some tiny spots where pixels didn't line up fully or were a bit jittery, nothing that'd ruin your experience but they did stick out to me during my playthrough. The music is phenomenal as you'd expect, maybe a bit samey at times, but better that than incohesive, a little more variety in some spots wouldn't hurt, and might heighten the impact of the emotional tracks when they come in, but again, nothing that'll detract from your experience. I played "A bird story" prior to this, and honestly I didn't quite get the connection, I mean, yeah, same character, it's a standalone look into a point of his life that's been abstracted, but for a chunk of the game I was just like "so she's the bird maybe?" But no, the bird is kind of just insignificant outside of "A bird story", which was kind of sad to me, but it is what it is, it's not like it ruined the experience for me. I think Asher could've done with a bit more character development maybe, more screentime, more moments with his family, but the story does go on a bit as is, so I'm not mad they didn't try to shove more in there; I [i]am[/i] mad about the walk speed though, it's just too slow, for "To the moon" I think it worked better because the environments were a bit smaller, sometimes you'd be on a long walk from one area to another, but having most segments be smaller walkable areas made the walk speed feel reasonable for the majority of it, here it felt like it was padding the length of the game a bit, a sprint button at least would've been appreciated, I'm not saying we need to be running the whole game, just a slight increase, because as is, I felt like the walkspeed alone added at least half an hour to my playtime, maybe even a whole hour. But overall, great game, I thought it was really sweet, teared up a little at the end, I had minimal gripes with the story, the art, the music, the gameplay, I'm not gonna pretend there wasn't any friction with any of it, but it's so minimal compared to the master craftsmanship behind the entire rest of the game that they're just insignificant. If you're not a narrative game type, or you prefer games with intricate gameplay mechanics, multiple routes or endings, maybe this won't be for you, but if you like a good story with some interactive elements, I think this is worth your time.

representative_reviews.title: In Stars And Time
representative_reviews.text: Playing this game was an experience I will never forget! :D The art and music draws you in, but the comradery between Isabeau, Odile, Mirabelle, Bonnie, and Siffrin as well as the twists and turns along the way keep you locked in. I had so much fun just reading the dialogue between characters. So much humor and charm behind nearly every interaction, even with the people in the town. Their friendship is an anchor in a world of chaos, and it's so wholesome despite the pressure they faced. I also liked how the battle system was based on rock. paper, scissors, even if it did make combat less complex as a turn-based game. My only gripe with the battle system was how tedious it became to battle over the course of the game. I eventually found an item that allowed me to circumvent some of the tediousness which was nice. My main complaint with the game is that there are certain parts that feel unnecessarily frustrating and difficult to complete. I would say Act 4 gave me the most trouble and I actually had to go through a walkthrough twice in order to finally pass it. The story, characters, art, and music make it worth it but it does feel a little too much at certain points even if I understand it relates to a core part of the story. I highly recommend this game! This is one of those games that can change your life by playing. I will never forget my buddies Siffrin, Odile, Isabeau, Mirabelle, and Bonnie ; u; <3

representative_reviews.title: Ikenfell
representative_reviews.text: Gameplay wise, incorporating timing is used to make players get more involved with the combat system. How engaging it is varies from person to person, though the pitfall of "losing a match because you mistime a single action" ala Virgo vs the Zodiacs is not present, which should give you a glimpse of the overall difficulty. Personally, I recommend new players to turn on semi-auto for the first few chapters to get a sense of the timing without trivializing everything. Though be warned that once you master the rhythm part, most boss fights become cakewalks. The boss fights are also pitfalls of the game: Because of the 3xN nature of the grid, a single enemy will be severely restricted mobility wise, which, combined with traps, allow for the players to pummel bosses relentlessly. There is also no mana, so resource management isn't a concern. This means that bosses are difficult not because of their own patterns or gimmicks, but mostly because they throw a bunch of minions at you, sometimes to the point of blocking movement altogether, though I guess that's the point. Of course, at any time players can press the "I win" button, which I applaud for inclusivity - video games are for everyone after all. Speaking of inclusivity, the story absolutely does that theme justice. So as to not get into spoiler territories, I'll just say that you have representation of all sexual orientation and genders: from lesbians, gay, straight, to enbies and genderqueer... It shows a more realistic representation of life, that your identities matter, and most importantly, that people can accomplish great things regardless of background. Though I do wish that their identities factor into the plot or their character arc a bit more, but it's within the developers' imperative to create a fully tolerant world free of bigotry, and I respect that. [spoiler] My biggest peeve with the game is its epilogue, in which Gilda and Maritte are stated to have broken up because they love someone else, but Gilda is still shown to be completely head over heel for her ex. It's good that they remain amicable and avoid the stereotype of breaking up, but is it too much to ask for a happy ending for Gilda. She's my favourite character and now i just feel bad for her. The little gay disaster is really relatable and it's sad that after an entire game of bottling up her feelings she didn't get even a confession scene to end her arc with :(( [/spoiler] Edit: apparently you can buy the entire game's OST on bandcamp, so I retract that part of my review.

representative_reviews.title: Long Gone Days
representative_reviews.text: I went into this game very much hoping that I would like it. I won't lie, the visuals alone were enough to sell me on it but ultimately after reaching the end point of this version I can say that it had little bearing on the efficacy of the game. [ GAMEPLAY ] So, what went wrong? Let's start with the gameplay. The combat works like this: You can either hit the enemy with a % chance to miss, or you can hit the enemy guaranteed at a cost. Like, a cost that only has an unreliable way of being renewed. The simplicity of the skills really, really leaves a lot to be desired. Apart from the distinct lack of strategy in a turn based military RPG (use multi-hit attacks on multiple enemies and heal allies who are dying does not count), this feels like an awkward way to handle combat. It's a subtle pressure for you to not use your abilities as much as possible because you never know when the next morale (MP) boost will come since it's tied to major story events, but at the same time, the game is easy enough that you can just regular attack your way through the entire game save for a few instances those AoE attacks become relevant. Personally, I kept missing chest shots and pretty reliably hit head shots so it gave the impression that it didn't really matter that much which one I picked. If I'm going to miss anyway, might as well chance it on the higher damage option, which worked out pretty swimmingly. The slowness of the combat combined with being generally unstimulating leaves it feeling very much like an afterthought. Seems late in development to revamp the combat system, but if there's still room for hefty change I'd strongly recommend it because as it stands, the gameplay is a chore to sit through. The fact that I can't distinguish who can equip which armor whenever I pick up new gear is mildly annoying... [ WRITING ] For a game that tackles some serious subjects, it certainly doesn't feel like it takes itself very seriously. Okay, sure, maybe a missed opportunity but not a deal breaker. What does it have to offer instead? Well, not a whole lot. Because of its wishy-washy, half-serious tone, any kind of grim or otherwise dramatic scene that is presented is undercut by non-committal platitudes that lacks any weight or emotion. Rather than provoking feelings that are genuinely moving or rousing, we get these sort of... deflated anime speeches that feel like they don't have anything real to say. This could be salvageable if the game decided to lean more heavily into comedy or other more light-hearted avenues to make up for this, but it doesn't do that either. Instead, it sits in this awkward middle of the road space where it's NOT serious enough to be a properly gripping tale of injustice and revolution, but it's TOO serious to be a fun adventure about friendship and growth. I think it's possible to do both honestly, but the writing is much too timid to actually push for it. The actual dialogue feels quite stilted as well, falling short of giving players the impression that these are believable characters, or even that we should be invested in them. Their speech patterns are just barely distinct enough to not blend together, and it's all kind of robotic overall. This is not helped by the fact that the personalities of these characters suffer the same problem as the story writing: Too serious to be fun to read, not serious enough to be compelling. I can't speak for the entire plot, but of the roughly seven hours I've played so far it's been serviceable, with some hiccups and questionable moments during cutscenes here and there. The story is fine, if a little boring, but certainly not remarkable. [ STYLE ] The art is very good, and aesthetically pleasing throughout. The music, not as much. The soundtrack used in this game isn't memorable or particularly even enjoyable to listen to most of the time -- it's just kind of there to fill in the background so it isn't dead air. But rather than fading out of mind, it pulls me out of the experience a little. Not much else to say here, the game would benefit from tighter direction of the music. [ CONCLUSION ] Right now, this is not a fun game. It is an okay game at best, and sometimes that's enough for the average player to squeeze enjoyment out of it. If this is you, don't let this review discourage you from at least trying it out yourself. Otherwise, I find that it fails to deliver quality on many fronts -- but not so much that it can't be redeemed. In my opinion, there IS a base of a good game here, somewhere. But it would take much reworking to transform this into something memorable. I can't say it's something I'm holding out hope for, but hey, anything can happen.

representative_reviews.title: Katana ZERO
representative_reviews.text: Rating: 8/10 This is an absolutely amazing game, and one that often gets overshadowed by more popular titles in the genre of kill-them-all-in-a-cool-way games. The mechanics are extremely fun, and the inclusion of a full-speed level "playback" in a game centered around slow-mo mechanics takes away the usual distinct lack of coolness that comes with slow-mo. However, I think what often gets glossed over in discussions of this game is the story. At its core, this is a fascinating story about PTSD and the military-industrial complex. At times, it can get a little too unncessarily edgy (by which I mean the edginess doesn't add to the story), but it piqued my interest overall. The only real criticism I can level at this game (besides the occasional edginess) is that it's too short. The mechanics and areas feel too brief to really sink my teeth into them, and far too much of the story is left up in the air. The developers have been working on a (free!) DLC, though, so here's hoping it will expand further on the interesting elements of the gameplay and plot!

representative_reviews.title: In Stars And Time
representative_reviews.text: If there one characteristic I'm certain on, In Stars And Time's writing takes out many dialogue flourishes and facial expressions to make the characters WORK, especially across many, many, many, loops. Those interactions changing across the loops is how I see this story suits itself to a game. On the flipside, I not so sure I felt like gameplay should really take this long, owning to how combat is "required" with a certain fast traveling resource that feels somehow separate from the story, and yet is part of the story. I suppose that resource is just-- not gelling with the story in a game technical sense. I suppose, the story doesn't have much interactions with that resource outside of the resource being used to force the player to battle enemies? Except, enemies aren't *the* problem, rather it is the environment that acts as the challenge posed by the story. Enemies are just there, with very little interactions compared to the environment. With that said, I enjoyed In Stars And Times for bringing out these lovable dorks of main party, and an excellent showcase of dialogue tricks... Oh, I suppose I should say the game does a lot with very little in regards to maps & music. Classic pitch shifting, hahaha!

representative_reviews.title: Ikenfell
representative_reviews.text: I'm sad to give this a negative review but as the game went on, it only got worse and worse until I couldn't take the game seriously anymore. The cast is entirely queer, including one person with neopronouns which is nice to see. The story and characters are generally very shallow, and around the midpoint of the game each chapter starts feeling monotonous as the plot takes too many twists and turns to have been planned out beforehand. Combat is generally enjoyable, though in the late game health pools start scaling up and it's hard not to want a defensive build when a couple bad timings could cost 3/4 of a party member's health bar. Assigning equipment is rather unwieldy, as there's too many choices that are hard to compare to each other and become obsolete every other chapter, as well as completely arbitrary weapon upgrades that are just a money sink. There's adequate accessibility options to both autocomplete action commands as well as fights themselves, and also an option to display content warnings which is very much appreciated. The ending solidified my negative review. representative_reviews.text: tl;dr -- The storytelling and the soundtrack are pretty good. The gameplay falls off quickly, starting from the mid-game. Early game is balanced well and enjoyable. Chapter boss HP scales exponentially and their damage scales linearly. Your damage from levels and your damage from gear scale VERY linearly. Which means your damage will get outpaced starting from the mid-game. Late game, the bosses start to hit you for 45-80% of your HP while you will hit them for 3-4% of their HP: If you build damage, you deal 4% and take 80-100% of your HP per boss hit. If you build tank, you deal 3% and take 30-45% per boss hit. Either way, the boss fight will take 60-90 minutes and will cycle through the same 3 mechanics. PRO TIP: enable "auto-victory" and click it often.

representative_reviews.title: Ikenfell
representative_reviews.text: This is a fine title if you're a really big fan of turn-based tactical combat, but the only 2 possible selling points - combat and story - leave some MAJOR holes. Combat- It's slow. Tedious and repetitive. Part of this is because of the "combat timing" interaction, where abilities have a slightly randomized pattern to make it harder to get perfect defense, but that really doesn't excuse it when increasing combat speed isn't an option. Some enemy attack animations (paper airplanes) can make a single instance of combat last for more than 15 seconds before you have the *option* to cheat for instant victory. Buffs and debuffs typically last 3 turns, and you're expected to use them a lot for any hard combat. Bosses almost always spawn adds to slow you down, have tons of health, and usually don't hurt. In some cases, they also have several dull phases. Further, characters can't aim sideways. There's no explanation given, but you're on a 3x12 or so board, and being next to a target is generally a problem. In the end, the combat isn't really difficult and doesn't require a lot of thinking. You keep up your buffs, debuffs, and wail on the enemy for as long as it takes to make combat end. Most items are prohibitively expensive to use outside of hard combat situations, and the only remedy for this status is copious amounts of stealing - which, again, extends each and every combat, and can only be done by 1 character. The story: Apart from major gaps in the story, minor characters steal the spotlight at the end for no apparent reason, few of the characters are actually likable, and there's a weird disconnect between how the avatars are presented in game and the apparent ages and actions of the characters themselves. The ending scenes don't even seem to relate to the events that occur during the game. The secrets in the game, after a ton of hunting, will lead you to secret bosses! These, like the others, generally aren't hard, but expect to take 20-45 minutes *each* to defeat. They will not offer additional story content or any fun lore/interactions. Negative ranting aside, the music in the game is genuinely incredible and worth listening to without playing the game itself. It might be the only reason I felt compelled to finish the game.

representative_reviews.title: Impostor Factory
representative_reviews.text: ....wait a sec, please.... *yourjaguarlover dabs his puffy eyes* ahem. I played the Freebird games in the wrong order. Or did I? In any case, I have now completed the series. It is a series I have a deep, deep love for and here's what I think (no spoilers, it would be a travesty to do so) Not for the first time, I (wrongly) assumed this would be an ancillary part of the series, a spin-off, a side-quest. In fact, it's the beginning, and the end and the middle and all of it. For *reasons* I am actually super glad I played this AFTER The Beach Episode because the way all the final pieces of this story clicked together truly blew my mind and left me so satisfied and ethereally happy, in the way that only understood tragedy can provide. If you aren't aware this, like all games in the series are basically visual novels with very minor interaction - but those interactions are crucial, critical to how the game delivers its timing, its drama and its heartfelt, sorrowful truth. I can't stand visual novels but Kan Gao delivers something I have never seen before or elsewhere, by making you not just a viewer but somehow an essential third party to it even though you do not appear in it. And in this instalment, more-so than ever, you are in these characters hearts and souls and stories - irrevocably linked somehow so you feel every single emotion and unfolded plot development (assuming you have at least played To The Moon and ideally some others) If you played games in this series, you'll know there will be sorrow, bittersweet tears and swooping joyous releases of emotion - this instalment delivers those in spades but also true horror, grief and awful awful tragedy as you feel part of decisions you wish you could take back. It's all a part of the journey that makes you feel so whole by the finale. I wax lyrical about these games, I know, and I also occasionally talk about video games story relevancy to art and literature. This series, right from the beginning of To The Moon is the ace card in that argument. I'd go as far as to say it's a genre in itself - a videogame only by rote of you using a screen and a keyboard to experience it, a movie that could never be made, a story so sprawling and intricate that could never be just written down in words. What seems like another RPG Maker, low visual fidelity follow-the-story is actually something that transcends other media for me in terms of experience. Even those pixel graphics contain so much nuance and detail, the sound - always just perfect and beautiful and intrinsic - those few key presses and mouse moves and clicks which are literally purposefully timed by a maestro. Ladies and gentlemen, these games ARE art. Kan Gao is a genius and a legend to me, I owe him so much as a person who plays all kinds of video games pretty much all of the time for bringing me something so different -unique even - and being the only person I have ever been happy to break my heart so many times and in so many ways. When we ask what makes a good videogame, the same is true as in any walk of life. Have a vision, work out whats needed to deliver that vision in exactly - the tiniest - detail you intended and never, ever compromise. There's nothing like these games and they are all 10/10 perfect creations to me. This one is a moving masterpiece that fits right in

representative_reviews.title: Long Gone Days
representative_reviews.text: Really tempted to jokingly label it as "Metal Gear Undertale". This is an indie JRPG that combined a pretty grounded for a JRPG scifi plot involving modern war... and also a story about friendship. Generally it sticks very closely to this older JRPG canon of having parties, equipment giving stat boosts, taking turns using abilities or attacks or items, travelling trough locales and engaging in dialogue, all that. It's faithful to older 2D JRPGs to a fault, despite more modern art style it can be pretty slow with animations, transitions and prompts to perform actions. During certain dungeon crawls there's a lot of air vents to crawl and each gives confirmation prompt if you do want to do it where a single interact would have been enough. A lot could have been done smoother, really. New ideas are playing safe too, like ability to pick where to aim in JRPG combat, avoiding armor at chance of missing or reducing damage further to hit a painful weakspot and make enemy skip turns. It's interesting but under-utilized, and the limited hit spot variety is sad, could have had stuff like shooting specific equipment to disable specified abilities or induce greater variety of effects. Now, the story: a naive but principled rookie soldier, fully raised in a militarized society of The Core subterranean state deserts after discovering he's tasked to kill innocents, convincing another soldier to flee with him, on his way encountering other characters he teams up with to survive and then confront Core's ambitions. It's... not too sophisticated and you can see quite some twists before the characters do so to be fair everyone feels lowkey naive. But it kinda feels like an anime, young adult adventure sort, so it works thematically? Personally my favourite bits in this one were the towns you visit and roam relatively free in, full of things to discover, tiny quests and scenes spent with main characters. There's even an aspect where you need a specific language speaker to actually communicate with anyone else which doesn't have major impact beyond "can only meaningfully interact after X joins you" but it does add believeability to settlements. This is fine. I guess if you wanna play a JRPG but wanna go for more martial theme this will do well. It's nothing revolutionary though.

representative_reviews.title: Vampire Survivors
representative_reviews.text: The part of my brain that enjoys roguelikes has been fried from over-stimulation, leaving me feeling like I just played the closest thing that exists to a gambling-less slot machine. The power curve is very unsatisfying. Most runs take about ten minutes to ramp up, give you 3-4 minutes of feeling strong, and then fill the screen with so much crap you may as well be looking at a Jackson Pollock. For all of this, the gameplay is minimal. There's a point in pretty much every run where you no longer need to dodge and can just afk, and it happens earlier than it should. I also find there's very little run variety. Items for the most part do very similar things with the occasional dud and gamebreaker thrown in, and most characters play as carbon copies of one another that feel arbitrarily nerfed/buffed based on their starting stats and items. There are some unique gimmick characters like Babi Onna who only fires her weapons while moving, but these are maybe like 4 characters in a cast of dozens. As it is however, this straddles a very awkward space where it's too involved to be an afk/clicker type game, and too much of a brainless flashy colours number-go-up game to lean more into its roguelike, compendium unlocking elements. It's cheap and it'll flood you with enough sensory input that for a while you can forget that you're going to die one day. At a similar price point, I'd rather just drink a beer and watch TV instead.
